### I did this


Built curl without any TLS backend and without `arc4random`. Examined the random number generation in `lib/rand.c` (lines 40-84).

The `weak_random()` function falls back to a linear congruential generator seeded with the current time using the classic glibc `rand()` constants (`1103515245 + 12345`). The seed is derived from `tv_usec + tv_sec`, making it predictable.

This affects digest authentication nonces, WebSocket masking keys, and anything else consuming `Curl_rand()`.


### I expected the following

curl should not fall back to a predictable PRNG for security-sensitive operations. Options:

1. Make a TLS backend a required dependency
2. Remove the `weak_random()` fallback entirely
3. Fail at compile time if no secure RNG is available

An attacker who can approximate the initialization time can predict all random values and forge digest auth responses.

### curl/libcurl version

curl 8.18.0

### operating system

Fedora Linux 38
title: Weak random number generator fallback when built without TLS

### I did this


Used curl with `-L` to follow redirects against a server that returns a protocol-relative redirect:

```
curl -L https://attacker.com/data
```

The server responds with:
```
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: //169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
```

In `lib/urlapi.c` (lines 1355-1362), protocol-relative URLs (`//host/path`) cause a full host change (`host_changed = TRUE`). The port restriction only applies to absolute URLs, not protocol-relative ones. curl follows the redirect to `https://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` and returns cloud metadata.

### I expected the following


Protocol-relative redirects should be subject to the same restrictions as absolute redirects — at least the port restriction and ideally an option to disable cross-host protocol-relative redirects entirely. This would prevent SSRF to internal services and cloud metadata endpoints.


### curl/libcurl version

curl 8.18.0

### operating system

Fedora Linux 38
title: SSRF via protocol-relative redirect URLs

### I did this


Used curl with an LDAP URL containing special characters in the DN:

```
curl "ldap://server/ou=users,dc=example,dc=com??sub?(uid=*)(objectClass=*))"
```

In `lib/ldap.c`, the DN (line 740) and attributes (line 799) are URL-decoded using `REJECT_ZERO`, which only rejects NUL bytes but allows all other byte values including LDAP-special characters (parentheses, asterisks, backslashes). These are passed directly to the underlying LDAP library without sanitization.

This allows injecting arbitrary LDAP filter expressions through the URL.


### I expected the following


curl should sanitize LDAP-special characters in the DN and attribute fields before passing them to the LDAP library. The URL decoding should use `REJECT_CTRL` instead of `REJECT_ZERO`, and the decoded values should be validated against RFC 4514 DN format.

### curl/libcurl version

curl 8.18.0

### operating system

Fedora Linux 38
title: LDAP injection via URL-DN decoding

### I did this


Built curl without `USE_LIBPSL` and made a request to a server that sets a cookie with a broad domain:

```
curl -c cookies.txt https://sub.evil.com/setcookie
```

The server responds with:
```
Set-Cookie: session=malicious; Domain=.com; Path=/
```

curl accepts this cookie. The `bad_domain()` function in `lib/cookie.c` (lines 318-336) only checks that the domain contains a dot — it doesn't prevent setting cookies for TLDs like `.com`. The `is_public_suffix()` function (lines 859-866) always returns `FALSE` when PSL is unavailable.

Any subsequent request to any `.com` domain (bank.com, google.com, etc.) includes this cookie.


### I expected the following


curl should reject cookies with overly broad domains even without libpsl. At minimum, it should reject cookies where the Domain attribute is a public suffix (TLD). Options:

1. Make libpsl a required dependency
2. Without libpsl, reject all cookies with an explicit Domain attribute
3. At least reject domains that are just a TLD (no private suffix below the TLD)


### curl/libcurl version

curl 8.18.0

### operating system

Fedora Linux 38

body:
Issue forwarded from Anthropic's OSS Scanner.

Repro and patches: 

[ANT-2026-AY0KT9UC.tar.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34468527/ANT-2026-AY0KT9UC.tar.gz)

```
============================================================================
ANT-2026-AY0KT9UC  [low]  CWE-178  logic
cookie prefix bypass via mixed case names
Location: lib/cookie.c:442  in parse_first_pair()
Commit:   705b02e4160bead0f274791bc446fae5d2b2b717
============================================================================
```

curl's `__Host-` and `__Secure-` cookie prefix protections can be bypassed by changing the case of the prefix. An on-path attacker answering a single cleartext request, or a server on a sibling subdomain, can get curl to store a cookie such as `__host-sid=evil` without `Secure`, or with a `Domain` attribute, and send it to the HTTPS site alongside the genuine `__Host-sid`. This only matters for sites that look up cookie names case-insensitively, which is the case RFC 6265bis has in mind when it tells user agents to match the prefixes case-insensitively. For such sites it allows session fixation or an overridden token; nothing is disclosed to the attacker.

The cause is that `parse_first_pair()` in `lib/cookie.c` (and `parse_netscape()` for cookie files) detects the prefixes with a case-sensitive `strncmp()`. The `prefix_secure`/`prefix_host` flags are therefore never set for `__host-sid`, and the checks in `Curl_cookie_add()` are skipped. The secure-overlay rule in `replace_existing()` compares names with `strcmp()`, so it also treats `__host-sid` as unrelated to the existing `__Host-sid`. The attacker needs the cookie engine to be enabled and their transfer to share a cookie store with the HTTPS transfers. The header path has been affected since 8.13.0 (5b5e2f7318, "cookie: do prefix matching case-sensitively", which reverted the earlier case-insensitive match from 14061f784c). The file loader has been affected since 8.21.0 (fdd6ba3580), though that half is not an attack path on its own. The attached reproducer runs one curl session against a loopback HTTPS site and a cleartext attacker. The correctly spelled `__Host-sid=evil` is refused, while `__host-sid=evil` arrives at the HTTPS site as `Cookie: __host-sid=evil; __Host-sid=good`. It does not show a server acting on that value.

## Details

curl applies the `__Secure-` and `__Host-` cookie prefix rules only to names that spell the prefix in
exactly that case. RFC 6265bis asks user agents to match the prefixes case-insensitively, so
`__host-x` and `__SECURE-x` get through as ordinary cookies.

With a jar that already holds the site's own `__Host-sid=good` (set over HTTPS with `Secure; Path=/`),
a cleartext response for `http://example.com/` carrying

```
Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=evil; Path=/
```

is dropped, because a `__Host-` cookie must be `Secure`. The same response with

```
Set-Cookie: __host-sid=evil; Path=/
```

is stored, and the next request to `https://example.com/` carries
`Cookie: __Host-sid=good; __host-sid=evil`.

The prefixes are detected in `parse_first_pair()`, `lib/cookie.c:441`:

```c
  /* Check if we have a reserved prefix set. */
  if(!strncmp("__Secure-", curlx_str(name), 9))
    co->prefix_secure = TRUE;
  else if(!strncmp("__Host-", curlx_str(name), 7))
    co->prefix_host = TRUE;
```

and the same way for cookie files in `parse_netscape()`, `lib/cookie.c:752-755`. The two flags are
the only thing that arms the rules in `Curl_cookie_add()`:

```c
  if(co->prefix_secure && !co->secure)                                   /* lib/cookie.c:1018 */
    goto fail;
  …
  if(co->prefix_host) {                                                  /* lib/cookie.c:1025 */
    if(co->secure && co->path && !strcmp(co->path, "/") && !co->tailmatch)
      ;
    else
      goto fail;
  }
```

For `__host-sid` neither flag is set, both checks are skipped, and the cookie is stored without
`Secure` (or with a `Domain`, or with another `Path`). The other safeguard on this path, "a non-secure
cookie may not overlay an existing secure cookie" in `replace_existing()`, compares names with
`strcmp()` (`lib/cookie.c:882`), so it sees `__host-sid` and `__Host-sid` as unrelated cookies. When the
request is built, `Curl_cookie_getlist()` selects both.

RFC 6265bis describes the prefixes twice. Sections 4.1.3.1 and 4.1.3.2 belong to the server
requirements and say what a server may conclude from a name that begins with a case-sensitive match
for the prefix. The user agent requirements (section 5) differ on purpose: the "Cookie Name Prefixes"
subsection says user agents must match the prefix case-insensitively, and the "Storage Model"
algorithm ignores a cookie whose name "begins with a case-insensitive match for the string"
`__Secure-` or `__Host-` unless it meets the prefix's conditions. The reason given there is that some
servers process cookie names case-insensitively, so for them `__host-sid` is `__Host-sid`, and the
example it gives is an attacker who sets a miscapitalized copy of a prefixed cookie.

curl's history on this line:

- 5af0165562 (2020): case-sensitive, citing rfc6265bis draft-04.
- 14061f784c (2022, 7.87.0): case-insensitive, "Adapted to language in rfc6265bis draft-11".
- 5b5e2f7318 ("cookie: do prefix matching case-sensitively", 2025-02-26, first in 8.13.0): back to
  `strncmp()`, citing sections 4.1.3.1 and 4.1.3.2 of draft-19, which are the server sections. This
  is the commit that introduces the bypass on the header path; its parent does not reproduce.
- fdd6ba3580 (8.21.0): the file loader changed to `strncmp()` as well; its comment at
  `lib/cookie.c:749` says this is "as the 6265bis document specifies", and `tests/data/test2311` now
  asserts that a non-secure `__secure-x` is loaded from a file and sent.

The header path is therefore affected from 8.13.0 and the file loader from 8.21.0. The file loader
half is not an attack path on its own (whoever writes the jar can already write a correctly spelled
`__Host-` line marked secure); it is the same rule and belongs in the same fix. The behaviour
above was observed on master (705b02e416) with the prepared Debug/ASan builds (OpenSSL 3.5.7 and
GnuTLS), and on non-debug builds of master and of `curl-8_23_0`. No debug-only code is involved.

## Impact

The prefixes let a site rely on a `__Host-` cookie having been set by that exact host over HTTPS,
not by a subdomain or by someone on the network path. With curl as the client and a cookie store
shared between the transfers, two attackers can plant a cookie whose name differs from the
protected one only in case: an on-path attacker who answers one cleartext request to the host
(shown by the reproducer), and a server on a sibling subdomain that sends
`__host-sid=evil; Domain=example.com; Path=/; Secure` (checked by hand: stored and sent to
`https://example.com`, while the same line spelled `__Host-sid` is refused). curl then sends both
cookies to the HTTPS site. Their relative order follows creation order and reverses every time the
jar is written and read back, so neither a first-match nor a last-match lookup on the server is
safe.

A site that compares cookie names exactly is not affected: it sees an unrelated cookie, which a
cleartext origin can always set. A site whose framework looks names up case-insensitively reads the
attacker's value as its `__Host-`/`__Secure-` cookie, which gives session fixation or an overridden
token, the attack the prefix exists to stop. The reproducer's site only echoes the `Cookie:` header
it receives; that a server then takes the attacker's value depends on such a case-insensitive
framework and is not demonstrated here. Nothing is disclosed to the attacker. The preconditions
(cookie engine on, an attacker-served transfer in the same cookie store, a case-insensitive server)
make this a low severity issue.

This is adjacent to CVE-2023-46218 (mixed-case domain defeats the PSL check, fixed by 2b0994c29a):
again a cookie acceptance rule that is keyed on one spelling. That one needed nothing from the
server; this one depends on how the server matches names.

## Reproducing

Run `repro` with its companions at `/tmp/repro.d`. It uses the prepared `/src/build/openssl/src/curl`,
and sets nothing beyond the curl options shown below.

Files and whose part each plays:

- `repro` is the user of the curl tool, and it holds the verdict. It also holds the two `Set-Cookie`
  values the attacker sends, which differ only in the case of the prefix:
  `__Host-sid=evil; Path=/` (the control) and `__host-sid=evil; Path=/`.
- `repro.d/cleartext_attacker.py` is the on-path attacker. It has no certificate for `example.com`, so all
  it does is answer a cleartext request for `http://example.com/` with the `Set-Cookie` value it was started
  with. One instance is started per value.
- `repro.d/genuine_site.py` is the genuine `https://example.com` (setup). `/login` sets
  `__Host-sid=good; Secure; Path=/`; `/account` answers with the `Cookie:` header it received as its body.
- `repro.d/start_servers.py` is the setup plumbing. It makes a self-signed certificate for `example.com` with
  the `openssl` tool, then starts the site and the attackers on loopback ports the kernel picks.

For each attacker, `repro` runs one curl command whose three transfers share the in-memory cookie store
(`-b ""` turns the cookie engine on):

```
curl -sS -b "" --cacert example.com.pem \
     --resolve example.com:SITE:127.0.0.1 --resolve example.com:ATTACKER:127.0.0.1 \
     https://example.com:SITE/login  http://example.com:ATTACKER/  https://example.com:SITE/account
```

TLS verification stays on (`--cacert`); `--resolve` maps `example.com` to 127.0.0.1. The output is what
`https://example.com/account` received. Expected on an affected curl:

```
CONTROL   attacker Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=evil; Path=/    https site then received Cookie: __Host-sid=good
OBSERVED  attacker Set-Cookie: __host-sid=evil; Path=/    https site then received Cookie: __host-sid=evil; __Host-sid=good
BUG
```

`BUG` is printed when the control attacker's cookie was refused (the site received only `__Host-sid=good`)
and the miscased one reached the HTTPS site. With the attached patch both rounds print
`__Host-sid=good` and the script prints `OK`. The two cookies arrive in the opposite order from the
header quoted under Details, which went through a jar file; the check does not depend on the order.

## Suggested fix

The attached patch matches the prefixes case-insensitively again, in both parsers of
`lib/cookie.c`: `parse_first_pair()` (line 441) and `parse_netscape()` (lines 752-755) switch from
`strncmp()` to `curl_strnequal()`, the helper the file already uses for its other case-insensitive
compares. This is an exact revert of the code changes in 5b5e2f7318 and fdd6ba3580. Setting the
flags where they are established is enough: the checks in `Curl_cookie_add()` and the
secure-overlay rule in `replace_existing()` need no change. The comment at `lib/cookie.c:749-751`
no longer claims that 6265bis specifies case-sensitive matching, and the comment in
`parse_first_pair()` points at the user agent rules.

Miscapitalized prefixed cookies that lack `Secure`, `Path=/` or carry a `Domain` are now rejected;
correctly formed ones (`__host-x=...; Secure; Path=/` over HTTPS, an already stored
`__SecURE-SID` with `Secure`) are still accepted. The patch extends `tests/data/test1561` with
three malformed miscased cookies over HTTP that must not reach the jar
(`__secure-SID=42345; Domain=example.com`, `__host-SID=42346; Path=/`,
`__HOST-SID=42347; Domain=example.com; Path=/`) and one well-formed `__host-sid` cookie over HTTPS
that must, and flips `tests/data/test2311` so that the non-secure `__secure-x` line in the cookie
file is no longer sent. Both tests fail without the `lib/cookie.c` change and pass with it, the 73
tests selected by the `cookies` keyword pass on the OpenSSL and GnuTLS builds, and with the patch
applied to a clean checkout the reproducer prints `OK`.

The section 5 wording of RFC 6265bis cited under Details could not be checked against the draft
text offline; it agrees with 14061f784c ("Adapted to language in rfc6265bis draft-11"), and is worth
one look at the current draft before merging.

## Running the reproducer

`low/ANT-2026-AY0KT9UC/repro`, next to this file, with its companion files in `low/ANT-2026-AY0KT9UC/repro.d/` (cleartext_attacker.py, genuine_site.py, start_servers.py) — the script reads them from `/tmp/repro.d/`. It was written by an automated agent and our check ran it as root in a privileged container: run it INSIDE A THROWAWAY VM, with the image `oss-scan-705b02e4160b` built by `bash build/build-image.sh`, from the archive's top directory:

    docker run --rm --network=none --privileged -u 0 -w /src -v "$PWD/low/ANT-2026-AY0KT9UC/repro:/tmp/repro:ro" -v "$PWD/low/ANT-2026-AY0KT9UC/repro.d:/tmp/repro.d:ro" oss-scan-705b02e4160b /tmp/repro

It prints its evidence; the last line is `BUG` if the issue triggered, `OK` otherwise.

body:
Issue forwarded from Anthropic's OSS Scanner.

Repro and patches: [ANT-2026-9ESFUCKT.tar.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34450071/ANT-2026-9ESFUCKT.tar.gz)

```
============================================================================
ANT-2026-9ESFUCKT  [low]  CWE-295  crypto
gtls: Extended Key Usage not enforced on server certificate chains
Location: lib/vtls/gtls.c:1557  in gtls_verify_cert()
Commit:   705b02e4160bead0f274791bc446fae5d2b2b717
============================================================================
```

curl and libcurl built with the GnuTLS backend never check the extended key usage (EKU) of the server's certificate chain. With default verification settings they accept a server certificate that its CA limited to `clientAuth` (or `emailProtection`, `codeSigning`, `OCSPSigning`), and any certificate issued by a sub CA limited to `emailProtection`. An attacker who has a network position between client and server, and who holds the private key for such a wrong-purpose certificate naming the target host (or for such an EKU-limited sub CA), genuinely issued under a CA the client trusts, can pose as the server and read and modify the transfer. The OpenSSL build refuses the same servers with "unsuitable certificate purpose".

The chain is verified in `gtls_verify_cert()` in `lib/vtls/gtls.c` with `gnutls_certificate_verify_peers2()`, which takes no key purpose. GnuTLS only compares the EKU against a purpose passed as a `GNUTLS_DT_KEY_PURPOSE_OID` element to `gnutls_certificate_verify_peers()`. None of the later checks in `Curl_gtls_verifyserver()` look at it either: time, OCSP, issuer cert, hostname and pinned key. A `clientAuth`-only EKU marked critical is accepted too. This is the backend's only verification path, so TCP origins, HTTPS proxies and ngtcp2 QUIC all share it. Origins and HTTPS proxies were tested; HTTP/3 was not. Untrusted or self-signed certificates and wrong hostnames are still refused, so only the purpose restriction is lost. The call dates from the original GnuTLS support in 2005 (first released in 7.14.0). The behaviour was confirmed on master at 705b02e416, on curl 8.23.0 and on Debian 13's packaged libcurl-gnutls 8.14.1. It is the same gap that 3f8f725d97 closed for Schannel in 8.21.0.

The attached reproducer serves certificates from a throw-away CA with `openssl s_server`. The GnuTLS curl completes both wrong-purpose fetches with exit 0 and HTTP 200, while the OpenSSL curl exits 60 on both. A patch and a regression test are attached.

## Details

The GnuTLS backend verifies the server's chain without telling GnuTLS what the certificate is going to be used
for, so the extended key usage (EKU) extension is never evaluated, neither on the server certificate nor on the
CA certificates above it.

A CA that the user trusts issues a certificate with `subjectAltName=DNS:victim.example` and
`extendedKeyUsage=clientAuth`. A server that presents this certificate is accepted by

    curl --cacert ca.pem https://victim.example/

when curl is built with GnuTLS: exit 0, HTTP 200, no option needed. The OpenSSL build refuses the same server
with exit 60, `SSL certificate OpenSSL verify result: unsuitable certificate purpose (26)`. The GnuTLS build
equally accepts leaf certificates limited to `emailProtection`, `codeSigning` or `OCSPSigning`, and a
`serverAuth` certificate for `victim.example` issued by a sub CA whose own certificate says
`extendedKeyUsage=emailProtection`; the OpenSSL build refuses all of them. A `clientAuth`-only EKU marked
critical is accepted as well.

This was run with GnuTLS 3.8.9 against: master at `705b02e416` (the Debug build and a build with
`ENABLE_DEBUG=OFF`), a non-debug build of the `curl-8_23_0` tag, and Debian 13's packaged
`libcurl3t64-gnutls` 8.14.1 through a small `curl_easy_perform()` program. All four behave the same.

The test suite already has a suitable certificate: `tests/certs/test-client-eku-only.pem` (SAN `localhost`,
`extendedKeyUsage=clientAuth`, used as a client certificate by test 2088). A test case with
`<server>https test-client-eku-only.pem</server>` and
`--cacert %CERTDIR/certs/test-ca.crt https://localhost:%HTTPSPORT/%TESTNUMBER` ends with 60 on the OpenSSL build
and gets past the handshake on the GnuTLS build (curl sends its `GET` and, with no `<reply>` in the case,
returns 52 for the empty reply).

The chain is verified in `gtls_verify_cert()`:

```c
/* lib/vtls/gtls.c:1557 */
  rc = gnutls_certificate_verify_peers2(session, &verify_status);
  …
  *certverifyresult = verify_status;
  verified = !(verify_status & GNUTLS_CERT_INVALID);
```

`gnutls_certificate_verify_peers2()` takes no typed data. GnuTLS compares the EKU only with a purpose that the
caller hands to `gnutls_certificate_verify_peers()` as a `GNUTLS_DT_KEY_PURPOSE_OID` element (`gnutls.h`: "It
will be matched against the certificate's Extended Key Usage extension"), and then reports
`GNUTLS_CERT_PURPOSE_MISMATCH` ("The certificate or an intermediate does not match the intended purpose
(extended key usage)"). Without that element the purpose is not part of the verification and a `clientAuth`
certificate passes; with it (see the fix below) the same two servers are refused.

Nothing after that call makes up for it. `Curl_gtls_verifyserver()` (`lib/vtls/gtls.c:1625`) goes on to check:

- expiry and activation time of the leaf (1715-1768),
- the OCSP status, only with `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS` (1770),
- `CURLOPT_ISSUERCERT` (1778),
- the hostname, with `gnutls_x509_crt_check_hostname()` (1814),
- the pinned public key (1823).

The hostname check does not help either. GnuTLS looks at the purpose there only for the CN fallback: a
`clientAuth` certificate that has the name only in its CN is refused ("certificate subject name
(victim.example) does not match target hostname 'victim.example'"), the same certificate with a `dNSName` SAN
matches.

`Curl_gtls_verifyserver()` is the only verification path of the backend. `gtls_verifyserver()`
(`lib/vtls/gtls.c:1857`) calls it for TLS over TCP, for origins and HTTPS proxies alike, and
`lib/vquic/vquic-tls.c:166` calls it for QUIC with ngtcp2. HTTPS over TCP to an origin and to an HTTPS proxy
(`--proxy https://… --proxy-cacert`) were run, with the same result: accepted by the GnuTLS build, refused by the
OpenSSL build. HTTP/3 was not run; it goes through the same function.

The other backends in this tree do restrict the purpose. OpenSSL does it by default for a client `SSL_CTX`
(observed above). For Schannel with a custom CA file the same gap was closed in 3f8f725d97 ("schannel: enforce
Extended Key Usage for custom CA roots", released in 8.21.0), which requests `szOID_PKIX_KP_SERVER_AUTH` from
`CertGetCertificateChain()`. No corresponding change for `lib/vtls/gtls.c` exists in the history up to this
commit; in `curl-8_23_0` the same call is at `lib/vtls/gtls.c:1499`. The call has been
`gnutls_certificate_verify_peers2()` since GnuTLS support was added in `6e6193938249` ("GnuTLS support added…",
2005-04-07), first released in 7.14.0.

## Impact

Only the GnuTLS backend is affected, and the attacker needs two things at once: a network position between
client and server, and the private key of one of the following, genuinely issued by a CA the client trusts.
With both, they can pose as the TLS server towards a GnuTLS build of curl or libcurl with default verification
settings:

- a certificate that names the target host in a `dNSName` SAN but was issued for another purpose, typically
  `clientAuth`. This is mostly a private-PKI situation: one internal root that issues both server certificates
  and client or device certificates, with looser rules about who may request which name for the latter because
  the EKU is supposed to keep them from being used as servers.
- a sub CA that is constrained by EKU only, for example an S/MIME intermediate. Its holder can issue a
  certificate for any hostname, and curl accepts the chain.

With such a key the attacker reads and modifies the transfer, including credentials and cookies curl sends.
Without a certificate from a trusted CA nothing is gained: an untrusted or self-signed certificate and a wrong
hostname are still refused. The EKU restriction is the only thing that is not enforced, and only with GnuTLS.

## Reproducing

`repro` uses the prepared `/src/build/gnutls/src/curl` and `/src/build/openssl/src/curl` as they are, and
`openssl` for the certificates and the server. Nothing is rebuilt; it listens only on 127.0.0.1:24441-24443.

Files and whose part they play:

- `repro.d/trusted_ca.py` is the setup. It creates the root CA that the curl user trusts (`ca.pem`) and the two
  things that CA issued to the attacker: `client_only.pem`, a leaf with `subjectAltName=DNS:victim.example` and
  `extendedKeyUsage=clientAuth`, and `smime_subca.pem`, a sub CA with `extendedKeyUsage=emailProtection`. It is
  the only code that uses `ca.key`.
- `repro.d/attacker_server.py` is the attacker. With the keys it was given it signs itself a `serverAuth`
  certificate for `victim.example` under the S/MIME sub CA; it also makes a self-signed `victim.example`
  certificate for the control. `serve()` starts `openssl s_server -www` with a given certificate, key and chain.
- `repro` is the user and the verdict. Every fetch is the same default-verification command, no `-k`:

      curl --cacert ca.pem --resolve victim.example:PORT:127.0.0.1 https://victim.example:PORT/

It first prints the EKU of the three relevant certificates as `openssl x509` reads them. Then:

- `CONTROL gnutls self-signed certificate`: the GnuTLS build must refuse it with exit 60, which shows it does
  verify the chain against `ca.pem`.
- server with the `clientAuth`-only leaf: `CONTROL openssl` (must be exit 60, "unsuitable certificate
  purpose") and `OBSERVED gnutls`.
- server with the `serverAuth` leaf and the `emailProtection`-only sub CA as chain: `CONTROL openssl` (same
  refusal) and `OBSERVED gnutls`.

If a control does not hold, the script stops with an error and prints no verdict. Otherwise it prints `BUG` when
the GnuTLS build finishes either wrong-purpose fetch with exit 0 and HTTP 200, and `OK` when it refuses both.
Expected output on `705b02e416`:

```

EKU of smime_subca.pem      : E-mail Protection
EKU of from_smime_subca.pem : TLS Web Server Authentication

CONTROL  gnutls  self-signed certificate          : exit=60 http=000 SSL certificate verification failed: certificate signer not trusted. (CAfile: /tmp/tmp…/ca.pem CRLfile: none)
CONTROL  openssl clientAuth-only leaf             : exit=60 http=000 SSL certificate OpenSSL verify result: unsuitable certificate purpose (26)
```

The attached patch asks GnuTLS for a chain that is valid for TLS server authentication in `gtls_verify_cert()`,

the new failure. `gnutls_certificate_verify_peers()` and `GNUTLS_DT_KEY_PURPOSE_OID` are available since GnuTLS
3.3, below curl's 3.6.5 minimum:

```diff
--- a/lib/vtls/gtls.c
+++ b/lib/vtls/gtls.c
@@ -1551,10 +1551,16 @@ static CURLcode gtls_verify_cert(struct Curl_easy *data,
   bool verified = FALSE;
   unsigned int verify_status = 0;
   long * const certverifyresult = &ssl_config->certverifyresult;
+  gnutls_typed_vdata_st purpose;
   int rc;
 
   *pocsp_checked = FALSE;
-  rc = gnutls_certificate_verify_peers2(session, &verify_status);
+  /* gnutls_certificate_verify_peers2() ignores the extended key usage, ask
+     for a chain that is valid for TLS server authentication */
+  purpose.type = GNUTLS_DT_KEY_PURPOSE_OID;
+  purpose.data = (unsigned char *)CURL_UNCONST(GNUTLS_KP_TLS_WWW_SERVER);
+  purpose.size = 0;
+  rc = gnutls_certificate_verify_peers(session, &purpose, 1, &verify_status);
   if(rc < 0) {
     failf(data, "server cert verify failed: %d", rc);
     *certverifyresult = rc;
@@ -1607,6 +1613,8 @@ static CURLcode gtls_verify_cert(struct Curl_easy *data,
       cause = "certificate signer not trusted";
     else if(verify_status & GNUTLS_CERT_INSECURE_ALGORITHM)
       cause = "certificate uses insecure algorithm";
+    else if(verify_status & GNUTLS_CERT_PURPOSE_MISMATCH)
+      cause = "certificate is not valid for server authentication";
     else if(verify_status & GNUTLS_CERT_INVALID_OCSP_STATUS) {
       cause = "OCSP status response is invalid";
       result = CURLE_SSL_INVALIDCERTSTATUS;
```

`lib/vtls/gtls.c:70`) were not tested.

The patch also adds test 2096, the case described in Details (stunnel serving `test-client-eku-only.pem`,
`<errorcode>` 60). It fails on the unpatched GnuTLS build with 52 and passes on the patched one; it passes on
the OpenSSL build either way. It was not run with mbedTLS, wolfSSL or rustls, which may return a different
error code for this certificate.

body:
Issue forwarded from Anthropic's OSS Scanner.

Repro and patches: [ANT-2026-2J7UJJL8.tar.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34449521/ANT-2026-2J7UJJL8.tar.gz)

```
============================================================================
ANT-2026-2J7UJJL8  [low]  CWE-416  memory-safety
HTTP/2 push on a DoH request: use-after-free in doh_probe_write_cb
Location: lib/vdns/doh.c:201  in doh_probe_write_cb()
Commit:   705b02e4160bead0f274791bc446fae5d2b2b717
============================================================================
```

A DoH server can make libcurl run its internal DoH write callback on an easy handle that has already been freed. This affects applications that use the multi interface with `CURLOPT_DOH_URL` and a `CURLMOPT_PUSHFUNCTION` that accepts pushes. The server only has to send a `PUSH_PROMISE` on the DoH request's stream and deliver the pushed body after the name resolve has finished; TLS verification of the server stays on. The attached reproducer shows an ASan heap-use-after-free read in `doh_probe_write_cb()`. In plain builds the observed effect is either a pushed transfer that fails with `CURLE_WRITE_ERROR` or, if the application does a second DoH lookup, the pushed bytes being appended to that lookup's answer buffer so that it fails with `CURLE_COULDNT_RESOLVE_HOST`.

The mistake is in `push_promise()` in `lib/http2.c`, which offers pushes to the application without checking whether the stream belongs to an internal transfer. `h2_duphandle()` then copies the parent's `CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION` and `CURLOPT_WRITEDATA` into the new application-owned handle. For a DoH probe these are `doh_probe_write_cb` and the probe handle itself. `Curl_doh_take_result()` frees the probe through `doh_close()` as soon as the answer is in, but the pushed stream lives on, so its next DATA frame reaches `doh_probe_write_cb()` (`lib/vdns/doh.c:201`) with the stale pointer. A push callback that replaces only `CURLOPT_WRITEDATA`, as both `docs/examples/http2-serverpush.c` and `http2-pushinmemory.c` do, needs no timing at all: the internal callback then treats the application's own object as a `struct Curl_easy`. Turning this into a write to a chosen address would need valid pointers the server cannot learn, so beyond the effects above a crash is the realistic worst case. The bug came in with 318bd978ea2d ("http2: init some callbacks for HTTP/2 push easy handles") and is in 8.23.0 and master. The curl tool sets no push callback and is not affected, and HTTP/2 server push is already deprecated, so few applications meet the precondition.

## Details

A DoH server that sends `PUSH_PROMISE` on the stream of a DoH request, answers the DNS
query, and sends the body of the pushed stream once the name resolve is over makes libcurl
call `doh_probe_write_cb()` with a pointer to an easy handle it has already freed. The
application only needs `CURLOPT_DOH_URL` and a `CURLMOPT_PUSHFUNCTION` callback that returns
`CURL_PUSH_OK` and leaves the pushed handle's write options as they are.

Observed at `705b02e416` (8.23.1-DEV) with libcurl built by clang 19 with
`-fsanitize=address`, `ENABLE_DEBUG=OFF`, OpenSSL 3.5.7 and nghttp2 1.64.0:

```
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free  READ of size 1
    #0 Curl_hash_pick        lib/hash.c:385
    #1 doh_probe_write_cb    lib/vdns/doh.c:201
    #2 cw_out_cb_write       lib/cw-out.c:191
    ...
    #7 Curl_client_write     lib/sendf.c:389
    ...
    #10 on_data_chunk_recv   lib/http2.c:1337
located 144 bytes inside of 2976-byte region, freed by:
    #1 Curl_close            lib/url.c:303
    #2 doh_close             lib/vdns/doh.c:1275
    #3 Curl_doh_take_result  lib/vdns/doh.c:1201
previously allocated by:
    #1 Curl_open             lib/url.c:457
    #2 doh_probe_run         lib/vdns/doh.c:280
```

The same server without the `PUSH_PROMISE` and the same application finish cleanly. The
same application against an ASan build of the `curl-8_23_0` tag produces the same report.

### How the internal callback reaches an application handle

`doh_probe_run()` creates each DoH request as an internal easy handle, stores its private
callback and a pointer to the handle itself in the ordinary write options, lets it
negotiate HTTP/2 and adds it to the *application's* multi handle:

```c
lib/vdns/doh.c:289   ERROR_CHECK_SETOPT(CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION, doh_probe_write_cb);
lib/vdns/doh.c:290   ERROR_CHECK_SETOPT(CURLOPT_WRITEDATA, doh);
…
lib/vdns/doh.c:296     ERROR_CHECK_SETOPT(CURLOPT_HTTP_VERSION, CURL_HTTP_VERSION_2TLS);
…
lib/vdns/doh.c:387   doh->state.internal = TRUE;
…
lib/vdns/doh.c:402   if(Curl_multi_add_handle(multi, doh))
```

Server push is a property of the multi handle, so the DoH connection announces it too
(`lib/http2.c:229`, `iv[2].value = !!data->multi->push_cb`), and `push_promise()` does not
look at which transfer the promise arrives on:

```c
lib/http2.c:831   if(data->multi->push_cb) {
…
lib/http2.c:838     struct Curl_easy *newhandle = h2_duphandle(cf, data);
…
lib/http2.c:869       rv = data->multi->push_cb(data, newhandle,
```

Here `data` is the internal DoH handle. `h2_duphandle()` copies its write options into the
new handle, which `curl_easy_init()` created as an ordinary, non-internal handle:

```c
lib/http2.c:738     second->set.fwrite_func = data->set.fwrite_func;   /* doh_probe_write_cb */
lib/http2.c:739     second->set.out = data->set.out;                   /* the DoH easy handle */
```

`CURLMOPT_PUSHFUNCTION(3)` documents this inheritance ("The new handle has the following
options duplicated from the parent: CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION(3), CURLOPT_WRITEDATA(3), …"), so
an application that keeps them expects its own callback. The same-origin check in
`set_transfer_url()` (`lib/http2.c:795`) compares against the DoH URL, which the DoH server
satisfies by naming itself in `:authority`. After `CURL_PUSH_OK` the handle is added to the
multi handle (`lib/http2.c:890`) and belongs to the application.

### How the pointer goes stale

The pushed handle lives until the pushed stream ends. The DoH handle does not: as soon as
the answers are in, `Curl_doh_take_result()` calls `doh_close()` (`lib/vdns/doh.c:1201`):

```c
lib/vdns/doh.c:1274      Curl_multi_remove_handle(data->multi, probe_data);
lib/vdns/doh.c:1275      Curl_close(&probe_data);
```

The connection stays open because the pushed transfer is attached to it. The next `DATA`
frame on the pushed stream goes through the client writer of the pushed handle into

```c
lib/vdns/doh.c:200   struct Curl_easy *data = userp;                              /* freed */
lib/vdns/doh.c:201   struct doh_request *doh_req = Curl_meta_get(data, CURL_EZM_DOH_PROBE);
…
lib/vdns/doh.c:205   if(curlx_dyn_addn(&doh_req->resp_body, contents, realsize))
```

`Curl_meta_get()` runs `Curl_hash_pick()` on the `meta_hash` inside the freed block. If it
finds an entry, that entry's pointer is used as a `struct doh_request` and the server's
bytes are appended to the dynbuf in it.

## Impact

The attacker is the DoH server the application was configured to use (or whoever controls
it); TLS verification of that server stays on. The application must use the multi
interface with `CURLOPT_DOH_URL` and a push callback that accepts the push without
replacing both `CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION` and `CURLOPT_WRITEDATA`, in an HTTP/2 build. The curl
tool never sets `CURLMOPT_PUSHFUNCTION` and is not affected. HTTP/2 server push is
deprecated and due for removal in March 2027 (`docs/DEPRECATE.md`: "barely any libcurl users
still use this feature"), so few applications meet the precondition. The server picks the
moment: it knows the resolve is over when the client connects to the address it handed out.

What is demonstrated is a read of a freed `struct Curl_easy`. What follows depends on the
heap. `Curl_close()` zeroes the struct before freeing it (`lib/url.c:302`), so while the
block has not been reused the lookup sees a NULL table and the callback returns
`CURL_WRITEFUNC_ERROR`: with non-sanitizer `RelWithDebInfo` builds of this commit and of 8.23.0
the same run ends with the pushed transfer failing with `CURLE_WRITE_ERROR` and nothing else.
That holds only for an application that does one lookup. If it does a second DoH lookup
afterwards, plain builds of this commit and of 8.23.0 reuse the freed block for the next
internal probe handle, with no heap preparation: the pushed bytes are appended to that
lookup's answer buffer (capped at 3000 bytes, so no overflow there) and that lookup fails
with `CURLE_COULDNT_RESOLVE_HOST`. With a single DoH server this gains the server nothing it
could not do by answering wrongly; with different DoH servers for different transfers, one
could disturb another's answer. When the block is reused by something else,
`Curl_hash_pick()` follows a table pointer and slot count taken from the new content; a write
of server bytes to a chosen address would need a chain of valid pointers at addresses the
server cannot learn, and the table index is randomly seeded, so a crash is the realistic
worst case beyond the above.

An application that sets only `CURLOPT_WRITEDATA` in its push callback gets
`doh_probe_write_cb()` called with its own pointer as the `struct Curl_easy *`. Both push
examples shipped with curl do exactly that: `docs/examples/http2-serverpush.c` with a
`FILE *`, `docs/examples/http2-pushinmemory.c` with a pointer into its own array. This
variant needs no timing at all; under ASan the callback reads past a 64-byte application
object. In a run of that variant the lookup failed and the pushed transfer ended
with `CURLE_WRITE_ERROR`.

8.23.0 is affected (same code at `lib/vdns/doh.c:289-296` and `lib/http2.c:738-739`,
confirmed by running). The bug was introduced in 318bd978ea2d ("http2: init some callbacks
for HTTP/2 push easy handles", 2026-09-30), first released in 8.23.0, which made
`h2_duphandle()` copy the parent's write callback and data. The probe handle had become the
DoH `CURLOPT_WRITEDATA` earlier, in 1ebd92d0fd (8.14.0), but that alone did not reach the
stale read: by reading, 8.22.0 gives the pushed transfer a clean handle and is not affected;
8.14.0 to 8.21.x copied the whole internal handle and were not shown to be affected.

## Reproducing

`repro` builds libcurl from `/src` into a temporary directory (clang 19, OpenSSL, nghttp2,
`ENABLE_DEBUG=OFF`, `-fsanitize=address`; ASan only makes the stale read visible), compiles the
application against it, makes a self-signed certificate for `localhost` that the application
trusts, and runs the application twice on loopback: once against the DoH server without the
push (control), once with it (attack). It takes about 40 s, nearly all of it the build.

- `repro.d/push_app.c` is the application developer's part: one transfer of
  `http://app.example:9080/` on a multi handle, with `CURLOPT_DOH_URL`, `CURLOPT_CAINFO`, its own
  write callback, and a `CURLMOPT_PUSHFUNCTION` that prints the pushed path and returns
  `CURL_PUSH_OK` without touching the new handle. The loop and the clean-up of finished handles
  follow `docs/examples/http2-serverpush.c`. `CURL_IPRESOLVE_V4` only keeps the DoH exchange to
  one request (A); the bug triggers the same way with the default A + AAAA.
- `repro.d/malicious_doh_server.py` is the attacker's part: the DoH server (TLS + HTTP/2 on raw
  frames, port 9443) and the plain HTTP listener its answer points at (127.0.0.1:9080). It reads
  the DoH POST; in `push` mode it sends `PUSH_PROMISE` for `/pushed` (promised stream 2, same
  `:authority` as the DoH URL) on the DoH request's stream; it answers the query with an A record
  for 127.0.0.1; it waits until the client connects to port 9080 (the resolve is then over and
  libcurl has closed the DoH handle); in `push` mode it then sends `HEADERS` and 64 bytes of `DATA`
  on stream 2; finally it answers the HTTP request with `hello`. In `nopush` mode it does the
  same without the two push steps.
- `repro` is the setup and the verdict: the build, the certificate, starting the server (it
  prints `listening` when its ports are bound) and the two runs.

Expected output: the `CONTROL` run exits 0 with `app: body: hello` and
`app: transfer done, result 0`. The `OBSERVED` run prints `app: accepting push of /pushed` and
`app: body: hello`, then the ASan report: `heap-use-after-free` in `Curl_hash_pick` called from
`doh_probe_write_cb` (`lib/vdns/doh.c:201`), on a block freed by `Curl_close` from `doh_close`
(`lib/vdns/doh.c:1275`) and allocated by `Curl_open` from `doh_probe_run`; the process aborts
(exit status -6). The last line is `BUG` only when the control run is clean and the attack run's
report is a `heap-use-after-free` with `doh_probe_write_cb` in the access stack and `doh_close` in
the "freed by" stack; otherwise `OK`. With the attached patch applied to a copy of the tree, the
same script prints the control output twice (no push callback, transfer done, result 0) and `OK`.

## Suggested fix

The attached patch stops offering pushes that arrive on internal transfers to the
application. In `push_promise()` they then take the existing "no callback" path, and the
promised stream is cancelled with `RST_STREAM` at `lib/http2.c:1041-1046`. This covers both
variants above (write options kept as they are, or only `CURLOPT_WRITEDATA` replaced), while
pushes on application transfers sharing the same connection keep working; changing the
`ENABLE_PUSH` setting in `populate_settings()` instead would not do, since SETTINGS are per
connection and a DoH connection can be reused by application transfers:

```diff
--- a/lib/http2.c
+++ b/lib/http2.c
@@ -828,7 +828,10 @@ static int push_promise(struct Curl_cfilter *cf,
 
   CURL_TRC_CF(data, cf, "[%d] PUSH_PROMISE received",
               frame->promised_stream_id);
-  if(data->multi->push_cb) {
+  /* pushes on internal transfers (like DoH) are never offered to the
+     application. The new handle would inherit the private callbacks and
+     userdata of the internal transfer, which has a shorter lifetime. */
+  if(data->multi->push_cb && !data->state.internal) {
     struct h2_stream_ctx *stream;
     struct h2_stream_ctx *newstream;
     struct curl_pushheaders heads;
```

The patch also adds regression test 2416 (`tests/data/test2416`, `tests/libtest/lib2416.c`):
a DoH lookup over the test suite's nghttpx HTTP/2 frontend, whose backend answer carries a
`Link: rel=preload` header so that nghttpx pushes on the DoH stream. It fails without the fix
(the push callback is called) and passes with it; it passes trivially if the installed nghttpx
does not push. With the patch applied to a clean checkout and libcurl rebuilt, the reproducer
prints `OK`.

## Running the reproducer

`low/ANT-2026-2J7UJJL8/repro`, next to this file, with its companion files in `low/ANT-2026-2J7UJJL8/repro.d/` (malicious_doh_server.py, push_app.c) — the script reads them from `/tmp/repro.d/`. It was written by an automated agent and our check ran it as root in a privileged container: run it INSIDE A THROWAWAY VM, with the image `oss-scan-705b02e4160b` built by `bash build/build-image.sh`, from the archive's top directory:

    docker run --rm --network=none --privileged -u 0 -w /src -v "$PWD/low/ANT-2026-2J7UJJL8/repro:/tmp/repro:ro" -v "$PWD/low/ANT-2026-2J7UJJL8/repro.d:/tmp/repro.d:ro" oss-scan-705b02e4160b /tmp/repro

It prints its evidence; the last line is `BUG` if the issue triggered, `OK` otherwise.

body:
Issue forwarded from Anthropic's OSS Scanner.

Repro and patches: 

[ANT-2026-0P4XA07H.tar.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34449361/ANT-2026-0P4XA07H.tar.gz)

```
============================================================================
ANT-2026-0P4XA07H  [low]  CWE-459  logic
SFTP (libssh2): stale reply on reused connection after post-quote timeout
Location: lib/vssh/libssh2.c:3222  in ssh_block_statemach()
Commit:   705b02e4160bead0f274791bc446fae5d2b2b717
============================================================================
```

When an SFTP transfer using the libssh2 backend times out while closing the file or running its post-quote commands, curl returns the connection to the pool with an SFTP request still outstanding. The next transfer on that connection gets the stale reply to the old request and reports `CURLE_OK` even though its download is truncated, its file was never opened, or its post-quote `rename`, `chmod` or `rm` was never sent. An attacker on the network path, with no keys and without changing any bytes, can cause this by delaying one encrypted server packet for a few seconds. A server that is simply slow on that one reply produces the same result.

The bug is in `ssh_block_statemach()` in `lib/vssh/libssh2.c`. When `Curl_timeleft_ms()` goes negative it returns `CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT` without calling `connclose()`. Because the transfer itself was not premature, `multi_done()` keeps the connection. The next transfer's call to the same libssh2 function, for example `libssh2_sftp_stat_ex()`, is treated by libssh2 as a continuation of the pending call, so it sends nothing and returns the old answer. A leftover `sshc->nextstate` can also make the next DO phase skip opening the file.

Triggering it requires all of the following:

* a post-quote command on the first transfer,
* an overall timeout that expires while that command's reply is held,
* another SFTP transfer to the same server and user that reuses the connection,
* the delayed packet arriving only after that transfer has picked up the connection.

The first transfer's error 28 appears only on stderr. With `--next` or several URLs, the curl tool's exit code is 0.

The attached reproducer uses a stock OpenSSH server with host key verification on and a relay that forwards every byte unchanged. It makes a plain download exit 0 after saving 11 of 8000 bytes, the size of the previously uploaded file. The attacker controls only the timing, not the data, and no memory is corrupted or disclosed. The code path was introduced in 684830cb2a2f (curl 7.21.0, per bisection). It reproduces on current master and on 8.23.0.

## Details

When `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT` expires while an SFTP transfer is in its DONE phase (closing the file, running post-quote
commands), `ssh_block_statemach()` gives up in the middle of a libssh2 call but leaves the connection reusable. The
connection returns to the pool with an SFTP request still in flight. The next transfer that calls the same libssh2
function on it sends no request of its own and is handed the late reply to the old one.

Shown with a stock OpenSSH server and a TCP relay between curl and the server. The relay changes no byte and only
forwards one server packet 5 seconds late. Host key verification is on:

```
curl --max-time 3 -T note.txt sftp://host/dir/note.txt -Q '-mtime "1 jan 2020" /dir/note.txt' \
  --next --max-time 20 -o report.csv sftp://host/dir/report.csv
```

- Nothing delayed: both transfers exit 0 and `report.csv` is 8000 bytes, as on the server.
- Reply to the post-quote `SSH_FXP_STAT` delayed: the upload exits 28 and `-v` prints
  `Connection #0 to host ... left intact`. The download prints `Reusing existing sftp: connection`, **exits 0, and
  `report.csv` is 11 bytes**, the size of `note.txt`. The `sftp-server` debug log of the session has one
  `stat name ".../note.txt"` and no stat for `report.csv`.

The exit that leaves the connection reusable, `lib/vssh/libssh2.c:3214`:

```c
    if(!disconnect) {
      result = Curl_pgrsCheck(data);
      if(result)
        break;

      left_ms = Curl_timeleft_ms(data);
      if(left_ms < 0) {
        failf(data, "Operation timed out");
        return CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT;      /* sshc->state != SSH_STOP, no connclose() */
      }
    }
```

Nothing later closes the connection:

- The loop is entered from `sftp_done()` through `ssh_done()` (`lib/vssh/libssh2.c:3780`, `:3620`). The caller is
  `multistate_done()`, which runs `multi_done(data, *presult, FALSE)` (`lib/multi.c:2700`): the data transfer itself
  completed, so `status` is `CURLE_OK` and `premature` is `FALSE`.
- `multi_done()` returns the error from `->done()` to the application, but decides what happens to the connection
  from `premature` and `conn->bits.close` only (`multi_conn_should_close()`, `lib/multi.c:598-636`). Both are still
  false, so `multi_done_locked()` returns `CPOOL_DO_IDLE` (`lib/multi.c:673`).
- For contrast, a timeout found by the multi state machine closes the connection: `multi_handle_timeout()` calls
  `streamclose()` and `multi_done(data, *result, TRUE)` (`lib/multi.c:1853-1859`). FTP covers the same situation in
  its own done function: when the final reply times out, `ftp_done_control_reply()` calls `connclose(conn)`
  (`lib/ftp.c:3755-3759`).

Two kinds of state survive on the pooled connection.

**1. The libssh2 request in flight.** A non-blocking libssh2 SFTP call that returned `LIBSSH2_ERROR_EAGAIN` has to
be repeated until it completes. In the example, `sftp_quote_stat()` (`lib/vssh/libssh2.c:1170`) has
`libssh2_sftp_stat_ex(".../note.txt")` outstanding when the timeout hits. The download then calls
`libssh2_sftp_stat_ex(".../report.csv")` in `sftp_download_stat()` (`lib/vssh/libssh2.c:1264`). libssh2 takes this
as the continuation of the old call, sends nothing, and returns the attributes of `note.txt` once the held packet
arrives. curl stores that size in `data->req.size` and `data->req.maxdownload` (`:1301-1302`) and ends the transfer
"complete" after 11 bytes.

**2. curl's own `sshc->nextstate`.** `sftp_done()` sets `sshc->nextstate = SSH_SFTP_POSTQUOTE_INIT` when a
post-quote list exists (`lib/vssh/libssh2.c:3794`). If the timeout hits while the `SSH_FXP_CLOSE` reply is still
outstanding, the value stays. On the next transfer, `ssh_state_sftp_next_quote()` follows it after the last
pre-quote command instead of going to `SSH_SFTP_GETINFO` (`lib/vssh/libssh2.c:1903-1909`), so the DO phase ends
without opening the file.

Outcomes observed with the same relay and server. In each, the second transfer reuses the connection and exits 0:

| reply held back in the first transfer | second transfer | result |
|---|---|---|
| STAT of `-Q "-mtime ..."` | plain download | 11 of 8000 bytes (the example above) |
| SETSTAT of `-Q "-mtime ..."` | download with `-r 0-9` | all 8000 bytes: the old STATUS answers the STAT, the size stays unknown |
| `-Q "-rename one.tmp one.txt"` | `-T two.txt .../two.tmp -Q "-rename two.tmp two.txt"` | no second RENAME reaches the server, `two.tmp` stays |
| `-Q "-chmod 600 one.txt"` | `-T two.txt .../two.txt -Q "-chmod 600 two.txt"` | no second SETSTAT reaches the server, `two.txt` stays `-rw-r--r--` |
| `-Q "-rm a"` | `-o b .../b -Q "-rm b"` | no second REMOVE reaches the server, `b` stays |
| CLOSE, post-quote list set | download or upload with `-Q pwd` | no OPEN reaches the server: empty local file, or nothing uploaded |

What was run, and what was not:

- Master `705b02e416`: the prepared Debug build with ASan/UBSan (OpenSSL 3.5.7, libssh2 1.11.1) against OpenSSH
  10.0p2. A non-debug ASan build and a plain release build give the same result for the example, so no debug-only
  code is involved.
- Builds of tag `curl-8_23_0` give the same result. `curl-7_88_0` has the same exit (read, not run).
  `docs/KNOWN_BUGS.md` has no entry for this.
- Introduced in `684830cb2a2f` ("SSH: corrected the inability to respect the timeout", 2010-06-02), first in
  curl 7.21.0 (bisected with an easy-API driver through the same relay).
- Not run: the libssh backend, whose `myssh_block_statemach()` has the same exit (`lib/vssh/libssh.c:2518-2527`)
  but is not compiled here; SCP, whose `scp_done()` uses the same loop. The `Curl_pgrsCheck()` exit just above the
  timeout also leaves the loop without `connclose()`, but it is unproven as a trigger: it is reachable in principle
  through a progress callback that aborts, and a low-speed limit (`-Y`/`-y`) did not fire in the DONE phase.

## Impact

An attacker on the network path between curl and the SFTP server, holding no key and modifying nothing, delays one
encrypted packet for a few seconds. Against SSH such an attacker should only be able to make transfers fail. Here
the transfer after the failed one returns `CURLE_OK` with a wrong outcome: a download cut to the length of another
file, a post-quote `rename`, `chmod` or `rm` that was never issued (an upload left under its temporary name, a file
meant to be private left world-readable), or a transfer skipped entirely. The attacker chooses the moment, not the
data: the stale reply is a genuine reply from the server. There is no memory corruption and no disclosure.

It needs all of: the libssh2 backend; a post-quote command on the first transfer; an overall timeout that expires
while that command's reply is held; and another SFTP transfer to the same server and user on the same easy handle,
multi handle or shared pool (with the tool: further URLs or `--next`). The held packet must arrive only after the
next transfer has taken the connection, because an idle connection with input pending is discarded at reuse
(`lib/conncache.c:1076-1081`); with the packet released earlier, curl opened a new connection and the download was
complete. The first transfer reports error 28 only on stderr: with `--next` (or several URLs) the curl tool's exit
code is that of the last transfer, 0, so a script checking `$?` sees nothing. Given this option combination, the
timing and the bounded effect, severity is low. No attacker is needed: a server that is merely slow on that one reply
gives the identical result (reproduced with the delay on the server side and no relay), so this is also a plain
reliability bug for anyone using post-quote commands with a timeout.

## Reproducing

Run `repro` as root (it starts `sshd`). It uses the prepared `/src/build/openssl/src/curl` (libssh2 1.11.1) as is
and the image's OpenSSH 10.0p2 `sshd` with its stock `sftp-server`. It takes about 16 seconds.

Files:

- `repro` (the user, and the verdict): creates an 8000-byte `report.csv` on the server and an 11-byte `note.txt`
  locally, then runs the command line from the report, once per try:

  ```
  curl --max-time 3 -T note.txt sftp://.../note.txt -Q '-mtime "1 jan 2020" .../note.txt' \
    --next --max-time 20 -o report.csv sftp://.../report.csv
  ```

  Host key verification is on (`--knownhosts`); `--connect-to` sends the TCP connection through the attacker's relay.
  `-w` reports each transfer's exit code and, for the download, how many new connections it made. The only
  non-default settings are the user's own `--max-time` and `-Q` post-quote command, both of which the bug needs.
  curl runs with `ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0`. The image sets `abort_on_error=1`, so a leak report at exit would
  abort curl and lose the buffered `-w` output. The unfixed curl reports no leak here. A curl with the attached patch
  does: LeakSanitizer flags libssh2 session memory from the connection it drops.
- `repro.d/on_path_delay.py` (the attacker): a TCP relay that forwards both directions unchanged and in order. It
  prints the stream offset at which each server packet begins. From one given offset on, it forwards the server's data
  5 seconds late. It has no key and changes no byte.
- `repro.d/start_sshd.py` and `repro.d/sshd_config` (setup): start `sshd -D` on 127.0.0.1:22061 with key login as
  root, and create the client key and the `known_hosts` file.

Steps:

1. The attacker watches one upload on its own and records where the server's packets start. A small SFTP session
   is strict request/reply, so the later runs end with the same packet sequence.
2. CONTROL: upload and download with nothing held back. The script stops unless both exit 0, the download makes
   0 new connections (it reuses the upload's connection) and saves all 8000 bytes.
3. Attack: the same command line, holding back one of the upload's last six server packets. The 5-second hold is longer
   than the upload's 3-second timeout. The ciphertext does not show which packet answers the post-quote `STAT`,
   so the script tries them in turn, starting with the last, and stops when the bug shows.

Expected output: one `OBSERVED` line per try. On this setup, holding back the last packet changes nothing. Holding back
the one before it makes the upload exit 28, and the download still gets all 8000 bytes. The third try holds back the
reply to the post-quote `STAT` and gives:

```
OBSERVED server data from offset 2889 held back: upload exit 28; download exit 0, 0 new connections, saved 11 of 8000 bytes b'0123456789a'
BUG
```

`BUG` is printed only when, in one try, the upload exited 28, the download exited 0 without a new connection, and the
saved file is exactly the first `len(note.txt)` = 11 bytes of `report.csv`. That means curl took `note.txt`'s size
as the size of `report.csv`. With the attached patch (checked with a non-debug ASan build of this commit plus the
patch), the upload still exits 28 in every try except the first. Every download opens a new connection and saves
8000 bytes. After all six tries (about 30 seconds), the script prints `OK`.

## Suggested fix

The attached patch marks the connection for closure whenever `ssh_block_statemach()` gives up before the state
machine reached `SSH_STOP`, on both early exits (the timeout and the `Curl_pgrsCheck()` error), and makes the same
change to `myssh_block_statemach()` in `lib/vssh/libssh.c`. This matches what `ftp_done_control_reply()` does for a
timed-out final reply. Errors returned by the state machine itself are left alone (the libssh2 call has completed
then, so nothing is in flight), as is the `disconnect` path. The `lib/vssh/libssh2.c` hunk:

```diff
@@ -3213,13 +3213,19 @@ static CURLcode ssh_block_statemach(struct Curl_easy *data,
     if(!disconnect) {
       result = Curl_pgrsCheck(data);
-      if(result)
+      if(!result) {
+        left_ms = Curl_timeleft_ms(data);
+        if(left_ms < 0) {
+          failf(data, "Operation timed out");
+          result = CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT;
+        }
+      }
+      if(result) {
+        /* giving up with libssh2 possibly in the middle of an operation, the
+           next transfer on this connection would get the outcome of that
+           operation. Do not reuse this connection. */
+        connclose(data->conn);
         break;
-
-      left_ms = Curl_timeleft_ms(data);
-      if(left_ms < 0) {
-        failf(data, "Operation timed out");
-        return CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT;
       }
     }
```

With the patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, the first transfer still fails with 28, `-v` shows
`shutting down connection #0`, the example and the rename, chmod and held-CLOSE rows end correctly on a new
connection, and without a delay the download still reuses the connection. The `lib/vssh/libssh.c` hunk is not
compiled here and needs a build with that backend before merging. Closing the connection instead in `ssh_done()`
whenever the state is not `SSH_STOP` also stops the reproducer, but additionally drops a healthy connection after a
post-quote command that merely fails (`-Q "-rm missing"`). No test case is included; one is feasible with the
suite's own sshd (`tests/sshserver.pl`) if its sftp subsystem is wrapped in a pass-through that delays one reply.

## Running the reproducer

`low/ANT-2026-0P4XA07H/repro`, next to this file, with its companion files in `low/ANT-2026-0P4XA07H/repro.d/` (on_path_delay.py, sshd_config, start_sshd.py) — the script reads them from `/tmp/repro.d/`. It was written by an automated agent and our check ran it as root in a privileged container: run it INSIDE A THROWAWAY VM, with the image `oss-scan-705b02e4160b` built by `bash build/build-image.sh`, from the archive's top directory:

    docker run --rm --network=none --privileged -u 0 -w /src -v "$PWD/low/ANT-2026-0P4XA07H/repro:/tmp/repro:ro" -v "$PWD/low/ANT-2026-0P4XA07H/repro.d:/tmp/repro.d:ro" oss-scan-705b02e4160b /tmp/repro

It prints its evidence; the last line is `BUG` if the issue triggered, `OK` otherwise.
title: [vuln] SFTP (libssh2): stale reply on reused connection after post-quote timeout

I found a four-byte out-of-bounds read in the IPv6 ECN branch of libcurl's QUIC receive code. I first reproduced it with a short synthetic control message, then confirmed it through a real IPv6 HTTP/3 connection using unmodified curl 8.23.0 and kernel-generated ancillary data.

The affected site is [`vquic_msghdr_get_ecn()` at `lib/vquic/vquic.c:615`](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/3163ec065643ba20709f190111f42c3e1fe95273/lib/vquic/vquic.c#L615).

For an `IPPROTO_IPV6` / `IPV6_TCLASS` control message, the code checks only that `cmsg_len` is nonzero before copying a four-byte integer from `CMSG_DATA`. On this system, a header-only record has `cmsg_len=16`, while the four-byte value requires 20 bytes.

**Reproduction**

- Build curl 8.23.0 with ngtcp2, nghttp3, GnuTLS and `-fsanitize=address,undefined`.
- Run an aioquic HTTP/3 server on IPv6 loopback (`::1`), port 44444.
- Use a public-libcurl application with `CURL_HTTP_VERSION_3ONLY`. Enable `SO_TIMESTAMPNS` on its QUIC UDP socket through `CURLOPT_SOCKOPTFUNCTION`.
- Request `https://[::1]:44444/` using `curl_easy_perform()`.

Linux returned a complete timestamp record (`cmsg_len=32`), then a header-only `IPV6_TCLASS` record (`cmsg_len=16`), with `MSG_CTRUNC=0x8`. The four-byte read crossed the end of the receive-control allocation.

```text
AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow
READ of size 4
vquic_msghdr_get_ecn  vquic.c:615
recvmmsg_packets      vquic.c:717
...
curl_easy_perform
msg_ctrl: [4192, 4960); invalid access at 4960
```

The ASan process exited 134. When I disabled `SO_TIMESTAMPNS`, the same IPv6 HTTP/3 request completed with HTTP 200 and no sanitizer finding.

The earlier synthetic test used a 16-byte header-only `IPV6_TCLASS` record and produced a four-byte heap-buffer-overflow read. The HTTP/3 result above confirms that a real kernel-generated truncated record can reach the same read through libcurl's public API.

**Environment:** Linux 6.18.57 x86-64, glibc 2.39, GCC 13.3.0, curl 8.23.0, ngtcp2 1.25.0, nghttp3 1.18.0, GnuTLS 3.8.3, aioquic 1.7.0.
title: QUIC: IPv6 ECN reads beyond truncated IPV6_TCLASS control data

body:
I observed a four-byte out-of-bounds read in libcurl's UDP GRO ancillary-data handling, using real Linux `UDP_SEGMENT` / `UDP_GRO` traffic and the unmodified curl 8.23.0 HTTP/3 receive path. I also found a packet-boundary regression when testing a length guard in isolation.

The read is in [`vquic_msghdr_get_udp_gro()` at `lib/vquic/vquic.c:556`](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/3163ec065643ba20709f190111f42c3e1fe95273/lib/vquic/vquic.c#L556). It copies four bytes from `CMSG_DATA` for a matching `UDP_GRO` control message without first verifying the payload length.

**Reproduction**

- Build curl 8.23.0 with HTTP/3 (ngtcp2 + nghttp3 + GnuTLS) and `-fsanitize=address,undefined`.
- Use a public-libcurl HTTP/3 client that enables `SO_TIMESTAMPNS` through `CURLOPT_SOCKOPTFUNCTION`.
- On a local aioquic server, send 16 UDP aggregates from the server's actual socket using `UDP_SEGMENT`: eight 1,024-byte aggregates containing two 512-byte segments, alternating with eight 1,536-byte aggregates containing two 768-byte segments.
- Let the client's normal `recvmmsg()` / `UDP_GRO` path receive them. These test payloads were deliberately not valid QUIC application packets; they exercised the transport receive path.

With curl's 48-byte control buffer, Linux returned a complete timestamp message (`cmsg_len=32`) followed by a header-only `UDP_GRO` message (`cmsg_len=16`), with `MSG_CTRUNC=0x8`. No segment-size bytes were available, but the reader still copied four.

```text
AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow
READ of size 4
vquic_msghdr_get_udp_gro  vquic.c:556
recvmmsg_packets          vquic.c:718
...
curl_easy_perform
msg_ctrl: [4192, 4960); invalid access at 4960
```

The ASan run exited 134. The no-timestamp control had no sanitizer error.

I also tested the downstream packet boundaries inside libcurl. With only a length guard and the original 48-byte ancillary buffer, the client interpreted those **32 real UDP segments as 16 packets**: each aggregate was treated as one packet because its GRO size was unavailable. With a 128-byte buffer, it recognized all 32 segments using the correct 512- and 768-byte sizes. Both instrumented variants completed the HTTP/3 transfer with status 200, so that result alone did not reveal the boundary mismatch.

In separate kernel-socket tests, `MSG_CTRUNC` was also set at 64 and 72 ancillary bytes even though the GRO field itself remained readable.

**Environment:** Linux 6.18.57 x86-64, glibc 2.39, GCC 13.3.0, curl 8.23.0, ngtcp2 1.25.0, nghttp3 1.18.0, GnuTLS 3.8.3, aioquic 1.7.0.
title: QUIC: Truncated UDP_GRO metadata causes a four-byte overread and incorrect packet boundaries

body:
I observed a one-byte out-of-bounds read in libcurl's IPv4 ECN handling during a real HTTP/3 request. This was with the unmodified curl 8.23.0 source, built under AddressSanitizer.

The read occurs in [`vquic_msghdr_get_ecn()` at `lib/vquic/vquic.c:596`](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/3163ec065643ba20709f190111f42c3e1fe95273/lib/vquic/vquic.c#L596). The IPv4 branch accepts a matching `IP_TOS` record whenever `cmsg_len` is nonzero, then reads one byte from `CMSG_DATA`. A header-only control message has a nonzero length but no payload.

**Reproduction**

- Build curl 8.23.0 with HTTP/3 (ngtcp2 + nghttp3 + GnuTLS) and `-fsanitize=address,undefined`.
- Run an aioquic HTTP/3 server on `127.0.0.1:44443` serving a 460,000-byte body.
- Use a public-libcurl client with `CURL_HTTP_VERSION_3ONLY`. Its `CURLOPT_SOCKOPTFUNCTION` callback enables `SO_TIMESTAMPNS` on the QUIC UDP socket, then calls `curl_easy_perform()`.

With curl's 48-byte per-message control buffer, Linux returned a complete timestamp record (`cmsg_len=32`), followed by a header-only `IP_TOS` record (`cmsg_len=16`) and `MSG_CTRUNC=0x8`. On the last slot of the 16-message batch, the byte read landed exactly beyond the `msg_ctrl` stack array.

```text
AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow
READ of size 1
vquic_msghdr_get_ecn  vquic.c:596
recvmmsg_packets      vquic.c:717
msg_ctrl: [4192, 4960); invalid access at 4960
```

The ASan process exited 134; I reproduced this three times. With `SO_TIMESTAMPNS` disabled, the same request returned HTTP 200 without a sanitizer error.

**Environment:** Linux 6.18.57 x86-64, glibc 2.39, GCC 13.3.0, curl 8.23.0, ngtcp2 1.25.0, nghttp3 1.18.0, GnuTLS 3.8.3, aioquic 1.7.0.
title: QUIC: IPv4 ECN reads beyond truncated IP_TOS control data

### I did this

With a cookie jar holding a Secure cookie scoped to a loopback host
(e.g. localhost), I ran curl through a forward proxy to that host:

`curl -x http://proxy.example:3128 -b jar -c jar -L http://localhost/`

curl sent the Secure cookie to the proxy in cleartext, and admitted a
Secure/__Host- cookie the proxy set in its response.

### I expected the following

curl should not treat a loopback host as a secure context when the
transfer goes through a forward proxy. The Secure cookie should be
withheld (as it already is for non-loopback hosts since b9702f8c48),
and a proxy-set Secure/__Host- cookie should not be admitted.

Curl_secure_context() (lib/cookie.c) OR-s the loopback literals in
after Curl_xfer_is_secure(), so they override the "proxied transfer is
not secure" signal. Looks like an incomplete fix of b9702f8c48.

### curl/libcurl version

curl 8.23.0

### operating system

Linux localhost 7.2.9-201.fc44.x86_64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Fri Oct  9 15:04:46 UTC 2026 x86_64 GNU/Linux
title: Cookie secure-context check ignores the forward-proxy transport for loopback hosts, leaking a Secure cookie to the proxy

body:
libcurl's TFTP state machine fails to validate state transitions against the
requested transfer direction, accepting opening server responses for both
reads and writes interchangeably. A malicious TFTP server can respond to a
download request in a way that forces the client into transmit mode, prompting
libcurl to consume and transmit data from the handle's persistent
`CURLOPT_READDATA` pointer - including data remaining from unrelated prior
operations, such as an HTTP POST request executed on a reused handle.

CWE.desc: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

title: TFTP direction confusion

body:
When an FTP wildcard `LIST` operation fails, libcurl omits the restoration
path meant for successful listings, leaving the write callback set to the
internal listing parser and the write callback data pointing directly to the
easy handle. Subsequent reuse of this handle triggers an immediate crash, and
cloning it via `curl_easy_duphandle()` copies this corrupted state into the
duplicate. If the original handle is subsequently freed, executing a transfer
on the cloned handle causes a heap use-after-free read against the dangling
handle reference; alternatively, reusing the original or cloned handle while
changing only `CURLOPT_WRITEDATA` (and omitting `CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION`)
results in type confusion, forcing the internal parser to interpret incoming
server response bytes into memory at the application-supplied write data
pointer.
title: FTP wildcard write callback mixup

contrary to expectations and documentation. A subsequent transfer on the same
handle still sends an `Authorization: AWS4-HMAC-SHA256` header to whatever URL
is set next, leaking state information.

Enabling `CURLOPT_CRLF` causes curl to advertise the raw input byte count in
the `IMAP APPEND {N}` literal while transmitting line-ending expanded data.
The server reads only $N$ bytes for the payload, causing the remaining
overflow bytes to be interpreted and executed as pipelined IMAP commands
within the authenticated session.

CWE.desc: Improper Handling of Length Parameter Inconsistency

title: IMAP APPEND plus CRLF conversion command injection

body:
An authenticated HTTPS origin can supply an HSTS `max-age` value that the
parser accepts, but time serialization later fails to process. On 64-bit
systems, extreme max-age values compute an absolute expiry within standard
time integer limits that exceeds calendar time structure bounds. During cache
saves, the original HSTS file is truncated before writing a temporary
replacement; when serialization fails, the temporary file is deleted, leaving
an empty or partial cache. Because the save error is silently ignored during
cleanup, curl exits successfully despite the data loss.
title: HSTS response erases persisted entries

body:
Importing a `includeSubDomains` parent HSTS entry before a longer-lived child
entry, silently drops the child. Consequently, when the parent expires, the
child's valid HSTS policy is lost, causing curl to issue unencrypted HTTP
requests rather than upgrading to HTTPS.
title: HSTS cache import drops longer-lived child

body:
When using ambient user credentials, an HTTP request directed to one origin
may be dispatched over a connection previously authenticated via Negotiate for
a different origin, leaving the request's intended credentials unused.
title: cross-origin reuse of a Negotiate connection

body:
With the wolfSSL backend, when CA caching is enabled and an
`CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION` callback replaces the trust store, libcurl can
silently reinstall the cached store after the callback returns. A certificate
trusted by the cached store but rejected by the callback-selected store is
then incorrectly accepted.
title: wolfSSL CA-cache hit overrides callback

# Private Organization Existence Disclosure via /repos and /activities/feeds endpoints

## Summary

Sibling to GHSA-prr9. The fix in PR #38145 added `reqOrgVisible()` middleware to `/members` and `/public_members` route groups, plus inline `HasOrgOrUserVisible` checks in `ListPublicMembers` and `IsPublicMember` handlers. However, two other endpoints under `/orgs/{org}` remain unprotected:

1. `GET /orgs/{org}/repos` (line 1721 in api.go) — registered at top level with only `orgAssignment(true), checkTokenPublicOnly()`, no `reqOrgVisible()`
2. `GET /orgs/{org}/activities/feeds` (line 1764 in api.go) — same, no `reqOrgVisible()`

## Vulnerability

The parent route group at line 1716-1774 only applies `orgAssignment(true), checkTokenPublicOnly()` — NO `reqOrgVisible()`. Endpoints with their own inline visibility checks (like `org.Get` at line 150-155) are safe. But `ListOrgRepos` and `ListOrgActivityFeeds` have NO inline visibility check and NO `reqOrgVisible()` middleware.

### Impact 1: Private Org Existence Leak

- `GET /orgs/{private_org}` → 404 (has `HasOrgOrUserVisible` check at line 150)
- `GET /orgs/{private_org}/repos` → 200 with empty array (NO visibility check)
- `GET /orgs/{private_org}/activities/feeds` → 200 with empty array (NO visibility check)

The differential response (404 vs 200) confirms whether an organization exists, even if it's private.

### Impact 2: Repository Count Leak (Authenticated)

`ListOrgRepos` calls `listUserRepos(ctx, ctx.Org.Organization.AsUser(), ctx.IsSigned)`:
- For authenticated non-members: `private = true`
- `GetUserRepositories` returns ALL repos owned by the org (including private)
- `count` from `GetUserRepositories` is set via `ctx.SetTotalCountHeader(count)` BEFORE the per-repo permission filter loop
- The permission filter loop (`permission.HasAnyUnitAccess()`) removes repos the caller can't access → empty response body
- But `X-Total-Count` header leaks the actual number of repos in the private org

### Impact 3: Activity Feed Leak

`ListOrgActivityFeeds` for unauthenticated requests sets `includePrivate = false`, so only public activities are returned. But the 200 response (vs 404 from `GET /orgs/{org}`) still confirms org existence.

## Affected Code

- `routers/api/v1/api.go:1721` — `m.Combo("/repos").Get(user.ListOrgRepos)` — no `reqOrgVisible()` in middleware chain
- `routers/api/v1/api.go:1764` — `m.Get("/activities/feeds", org.ListOrgActivityFeeds)` — no `reqOrgVisible()` in middleware chain
- `routers/api/v1/user/repo.go:142` — `ListOrgRepos` calls `listUserRepos` with no org visibility check
- `routers/api/v1/org/org.go:453` — `ListOrgActivityFeeds` has no org visibility check

## Fix

Add `reqOrgVisible()` to both routes, or add inline `HasOrgOrUserVisible` checks in both handlers, matching the pattern used in `org.Get` (line 150) and the PR #38145 fix for `ListPublicMembers`.

Alternatively, move `reqOrgVisible()` to the parent route group at line 1716 so ALL sub-routes are protected.

## Severity

Medium (CVSS 5.3) — Information disclosure of private org existence and repo count. No user data or repo content is leaked.
title: Private Organization Existence Disclosure via /repos and /activities/feeds endpoints (sibling to GHSA-prr9)
